metadata.note: CLI explainer (cli-explainer skill — ADVANCED tier), built on D:\ai1-cli-main per CLAUDE.md rule 3. Folder dated 2026-09-08 per explicit instruction. Follows the mandatory CLI spine: INTRO → PROBLEM → CLI/CODE/OUTPUT → revision cycle CLI/CODE/OUTPUT → SUMMARY → NEXT STEPS → OUTRO; THE REVISION LAW satisfied by one full revision cycle. ACTUAL-CODE LAW: code/ holds four REAL runnable scripts (corpus.py, encoder.py, bm25_search.py, hybrid_search.py); both CODE beats quote them verbatim and every number in every OUTPUT beat is captured stdout, saved as _run-bm25.txt and _run-hybrid.txt. Dense retrieval uses REAL all-MiniLM-L6-v2 weights from the local HuggingFace cache — encoder.py parses safetensors and runs the 6-layer BERT forward pass in numpy because sentence-transformers is not installed here; validated behaviourally (identical 1.000 / paraphrase 0.555 / unrelated 0.100). Nothing is hand-tuned. THE FINDING IS NOT THE TIDY ONE and the reel says so: dense won BOTH queries, and the fused hybrid LOST the paraphrase by 0.00025 — which independently reproduces the chapter's own refusal to claim hybrid always wins. B04 reuses CliRunOutput and B09 reuses RagExecutiveSummary, props-only. B01/B07/B08 are three new bespoke components (RetrievalTwoQueries, RetrievalMatrix, RrfMargin) — GATE L searched four ways and every close lead (BrandDriftCaseStudy, CwcEvalScoring, CadencesFig3Artifacts) exposes only sparkLine/activeColumn, i.e. content hardcoded to another reel. beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — the ask lands answered.
beats.narration_text: Konnichiwa — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Chapter five made search fast. Chapter six asks whether comparing embeddings is even the right way to match in the first place — because there are two genuinely different ways to decide whether a chunk answers a question, and each one fails exactly where the other works.

props.command: Two employees ask about the same tuition policy. One quotes the code TR-114. One says "help pay for grad school". Which retrieval method finds the right chunk for BOTH?
output: each one fails exactly where the other works

beats.role_note: Mandatory PROBLEM beat: the stakes, stated BEFORE any prompt. Rebuilds the chapter's worked-example premise.
beats.narration_text: Here is the problem, and it is the chapter's own example. Two employees, the same tuition-reimbursement policy, two completely different questions. The first quotes an exact code: T-R-one-fourteen. The second never says tuition, or reimbursement, or policy at all — just, does the company help pay for grad school. Same answer. Opposite questions.

right/bottom card lands: the paraphrase question
the connector draws — both point at one chunk
the TR-114 policy chunk lands in terracotta beneath them

props.targetText: The company reimburses approved degree coursework up to $5,250 per calendar year. Employees must be full-time and receive a grade of B or better.
props.caption: Chapter 6's worked example: one gold passage, two queries with almost nothing in common.

beats.narration_text: The ask: sparse retrieval, from scratch. B-M-twenty-five — term frequency, inverse document frequency, length normalisation, and saturation, so a word repeated fifty times doesn't count fifty times. One detail matters more than it looks: tokenise so T-R-one-fourteen survives as a single term. Split it into t-r and one-fourteen, and the exact-match signal is gone before we start.

show.event: Spark greeting 'The ask,' holds
Command types — note the tokenisation requirement at the end
Send arms; runningText 'generating script…'

props.segment: Watch The Right Answer Get Outvoted.
props.command: claude "write bm25_search.py — BM25 from scratch over 12 help-desk policy passages, with IDF, length normalisation and term-frequency saturation. Tokenise so TR-114 stays ONE term. Run both queries and report whether top-1 is the gold passage."

beats.narration_text: Read the scoring function. Every query term contributes its inverse document frequency, scaled by how often it appears in this passage — and that contribution saturates, so repetition stops paying. The normaliser divides by document length, so a long passage can't win just by being long. And T-R-one-fourteen appears in exactly one of twelve passages, which gives it the highest I-D-F in the collection.

show.event: Code card lands, filename in the title bar
the TOKEN regex — hyphens kept inside a term, so TR-114 survives
idf() — rare terms score far higher than common ones
spark line settles: rare words carry the weight

props.title: bm25_search.py — Claude Code output

beats.narration_text: Run it. The code query: T-R-one-fourteen wins at three point four nine, ahead of two other policies that also contain the word reimbursement. Sparse nails it. Now the paraphrase: help pay for grad school returns the certification-exam policy, at three point eight two, because that passage literally contains the words company pays. The right answer is third. That is the paraphrase gap, measured.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — the second cycle begins here.
beats.narration_text: The revision. Add dense retrieval — real MiniLM embeddings, matching on meaning instead of words. Then fuse the two rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: each candidate scores one over sixty plus its rank, in every list it appears in, summed. Ranks, not scores, because B-M-twenty-five scores and cosine similarities are not on a comparable scale. And report all three methods.

show.event: Spark greeting 'The change,' holds
Revised command types — dense retriever plus RRF fusion
Send arms; runningText 'updating…'

props.segment: Watch The Right Answer Get Outvoted.
props.command: claude "now add dense retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and fuse the two rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, k=60. Report top-1 for sparse, dense AND hybrid on both queries."

beats.narration_text: Two pieces. Dense: embed the query, dot it against every passage embedding — the vectors are normalised, so that dot product is cosine similarity. Then fusion: for every ranked list a candidate appears in, add one over sixty plus its rank. No weights. No tuning. That is the whole of Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and it is four lines long.

show.event: Revised code card lands
rrf() — ranks summed as reciprocals, no weights anywhere
the dense scores line — cosine via dot product
spark line settles: ranks, not scores

props.title: hybrid_search.py — dense, then fusion

beats.role_note: The result, and it is NOT the expected one. Real data from _run-hybrid.txt.
beats.narration_text: And here is the result I did not expect. Dense got both. It found T-R-one-fourteen for the code query too, at zero point six — the entity-centric weakness the chapter warns about did not show up at twelve passages. And the hybrid, the combination that is supposed to be the safe default, missed the paraphrase. Only plain dense went two for two.

shot.visual_intent: a three-by-two matrix of methods against query kinds, hit or miss, with the surprising hybrid miss as the one accent

show.event: column headers land: exact code · paraphrase · both
sparse row resolves — HIT, MISS, no
dense row resolves — HIT, HIT, YES
hybrid row resolves — HIT, then the accented MISS

props.headline: Only One Method Got Both.
props.caption: Top-1 on the gold passage, measured by this reel's own hybrid_search.py over 12 passages. The hybrid miss is the surprise.

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — the arithmetic of the failure, shown. Also the native rebuild of the chapter's Fig. 02.
beats.narration_text: Here is why. On the paraphrase, the certification policy was sparse's number one and dense's number two. The right answer was dense's number one — but sparse had it third. One over sixty-one plus one over sixty-two beats one over sixty-three plus one over sixty-one, by a quarter of one thousandth. Fusion did not reason about either list. It counted ranks, and a confidently wrong ranking outvoted a correct one.

shot.visual_intent: the two candidates' rank contributions written out as reciprocals and summed, with the correct answer that lost marked in terracotta and the margin stated beneath

show.event: the paraphrase query pins to the top
CE-118 row: sparse #1 + dense #2 → 0.03252
TR-114 row in terracotta: sparse #3 + dense #1 → 0.03227
the margin settles beneath: 0.00025 apart

props.headline: Outvoted By A Quarter Of A Thousandth.
props.query: Does the company help pay for grad school?
props.marginLabel: 0.00025 apart — the wrong passage wins the fusion
props.caption: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) across both lists. It has no way to know that sparse was confidently wrong.
props.citation: Cormack, Clarke & Buettcher, 2009 · redrawn from the chapter's Fig. 02

beats.role_note: Mandatory SUMMARY beat — the lesson, honestly, including what this run does NOT prove.
beats.narration_text: So: sparse matches words, and misses paraphrases. Dense matches meaning, and here missed nothing. Hybrid usually helps and rarely hurts — but usually is doing real work in that sentence, and this run is one of the times it hurt. Two honest limits: twelve passages is too small to reproduce dense retrieval's known weakness on rare entities, and one fusion loss is not a verdict on fusion. The chapter says the same thing — the honest summary is not that hybrid always wins.

show.event: Headline types in: 'Usually is doing real work.'
Subline resolves: the two failure modes are complementary, the fusion is not free
Spark line settles

props.headline: “Usually” is doing real work.
props.subline: Sparse and dense fail on different queries, so combining them usually helps and rarely hurts — but fusion counts ranks rather than reasoning, so a confidently wrong retriever can still outvote a correct one.
props.sparkLine: Measure it on your own queries.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Take my own document set and build all three retrievers — sparse, dense, and a fused hybrid. Then find me the queries where the hybrid is WORSE than its best single retriever, and show me the rank arithmetic that made it lose.' That second sentence is the one that earns its keep. Anything will report an average that makes fusion look good; asking for the cases where it loses, plus the arithmetic, is what turns a default into a decision you can actually defend.
